cover.alt: Ásta sits on Manga’s bed crying and holding her cap without its tassel. Guðrún is beside her, Siggi by the door and Óli searching under a bed.
cover.art_brief: Ink and watercolour, established Kvöldvakan visual bible, morning in February 1876, baðstofa at Hamrar. Ásta, six, sits on Manga’s bed holding her black knitted skotthúfa whose tassel is gone, crying. Guðrún stands beside her looking at the cap. Siggi stands by the door with one hand in his pocket. Óli looks under a bed. No visible knife in Siggi’s hand, no recovered tassel holder, no lettering, no modern objects.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Ásta spurði: „Hvernig eru dvergar?“ Afi sagði: „Tröll eru stór, en dvergar eru litlir. Þeir búa í steinum.“
Brokkur og Eitri voru góðir smiðir. Þeir smíðuðu góða hluti fyrir goðin.
Siggi tálgaði skúfhólk úr tré. Ásta sagði: „Siggi er dvergurinn okkar!“ Óli sagði: „Hann smíðar eins og dvergur.“
Maður kallar við stóran stein, og steinninn kallar aftur. Það heitir dvergmál. Menn sögðu: „Dvergar búa í steininum.“
words_with_history.note_en: Dvergmál literally means “dwarf-speech”: an echo. [?] In Snorri’s myth dwarves live in rocks. The last paragraph presents the traditional image, not a claim that dwarves exist. Dvergmál is an incidental explained here, not an extra vocabulary or exercise target.

pronunciation_note.rule: In allur, gullinn and fallegur, ll is [tl], a t-like release into l; the sequence can be voiceless [tɬ] in other positions. This is not a rule for every written ll. In hvaða, hv is [kv]. Á in háls and tálga is [au]. In höfuð, ö is a rounded front vowel [œ]; final ð after u is soft [ð].

grammar.title: Góður · góð · gott
grammar.rule: „Þeir smíðuðu líka gott skip og langt spjót.“ · „Ég týndi skúfnum mínum!“ · „Ég sjálfur.“
grammar.note_en:
An adjective describes a noun; strong declension is the set of endings normally used with an indefinite noun (one without the definite article), and in predicates such as “the handle was short”. Weak endings after a definite article belong to G16. These tables show only cells attested in this story, with segment references. A dash means “not shown here”, not “no form exists”. The first table is singular; the second plural. Case shows a word’s role: nominative for a subject or predicate, accusative often for an object, dative after certain verbs/prepositions, genitive for possession and after words such as vegna, “because of”. Gender and number agree with the noun.

Góður skúfhólkur (s139), “a good tassel holder”, is masculine nominative singular; góð gjöf (s115), “a good gift”, feminine; stórt skip (s076), “a large ship”, neuter. In the accusative, lítinn hníf (s022) is “a small knife”, gott skip og langt spjót (s074), “a good ship and a long spear”. Góða hluti (s072), “good things”, and gullna bursta (s086), “golden bristles”, are masculine accusative PLURAL; this -a is plural, not feminine singular. Góðir smiðir (s078) means “good smiths”; tröll eru stór (s072), “trolls are large”. The story does not demonstrate every gender in every case, or a full góður paradigm.

Ending reference only, not extra exercise cells: regular strong accusative singular often contrasts masculine -an, feminine -a, neuter -t (góðan/góða/gott: “good”, agreeing with the object). Dative singular commonly has masculine -um, feminine -ri, neuter -u; genitive masculine/neuter -s and feminine -rar. Stems and consonants can change: litlum skúfhólki (s009), “in a small tassel holder”, hvítri ull (s108), “white wool” after af, and nýju hári (s068), “new hair”, illustrate dative gender; stórum tárum (s035), “with large tears”, is neuter dative PLURAL. Lítils skúfs (s112), “of/because of a small tassel”, gives masculine genitive; the corresponding regular reference forms góðs/góðrar mean “of good …” and are not story cells. No absent genitive or possessive cell is a drill target.

A possessive says who owns something. In the story it follows the noun and agrees with the thing owned, not its owner: skúfurinn minn (s032), “my tassel”; húfan mín (s053), “my cap”; hárið mitt (s010), “my hair”; húfuna mína (s143), “onto my cap”; skúfnum mínum (s034), “my tassel”, dative after týna, “lose”; kindinni minni (s111), “my ewe”, dative after af, “from”. Höfuðið þitt (s097) means “your head”; hann er þinn (s134), “it is yours”, refers to the masculine holder. Unlike minn and þinn, okkar, “our”, and ykkar, “your (plural)”, never change: dvergurinn okkar (s137), “our dwarf”; leikurinn ykkar (s055), “your game”, addressed to Siggi and Óli.

Allur agrees too: allir (s017), “everyone”; allt hárið (s064), “all the hair”; allan daginn (s059), “all day”; allar gjafirnar (s094), “all the gifts”; alla vikuna (s123), “all week”; öllum (s136), “to everyone”. Neuter allt can also stand alone: fer allt illa (s082), “everything goes badly”. Sjálfur adds emphasis, “myself/himself”: ég sjálfur (s044), “I myself”; Siggi tálgaði hann sjálfur (s130), “Siggi carved it himself”. Sjálfur agrees with the person it emphasises (here masculine singular: ég, Siggi). It is not the reflexive pronoun, which comes later.

The myth’s relative and causal clauses, the closed “look!” command, and predicative bestur, “best”, remain supported reading items. They are not apparatus production targets. Eins og (s138), “like/as”, is now vocabulary; ætla að with an infinitive remains productive from G14. This is not a Hluti-final cumulative reference.
